result: The experimental setup involved nine mice exploring an elevated platform with alternating visual patterns (vp1 and vp2) over forty 2-min trials. Recordings were obtained from 944 neurons across 167 sessions, with most recording sites (63.0%) located in the MEC, particularly in layer II (82.4% of MEC sites).
evaluation: Claims C1-C8 provide a comprehensive description of the experimental design, recording locations, and dataset size. The histological verification of recording sites and the detailed protocol description support the validity of the experimental approach.

result: HD cells (N=93) were identified using strict criteria (HD score >0.4, peak firing rate >5 Hz, directional distributive ratio >0.2). These cells showed similar directional tuning, firing rates, and randomly distributed preferred directions during both vp1 and vp2 trials, with comparable mouse behavior between trial types.
evaluation: Claims C9-C16 establish rigorous identification criteria for HD cells and demonstrate baseline stability across trial types. The use of directional distributive ratio (C10) appropriately controls for spatial selectivity confounds. Statistical tests support the lack of systematic differences between trial types at the population level.

result: HD cells in the MEC/PaS exhibit bimodal theta rhythmicity, with Gaussian mixture modeling identifying two distinct populations: non-rhythmic (N=34) and theta-rhythmic (N=59) cells, with a theta index threshold of 0.07.
evaluation: Claims C17-C20 demonstrate a novel finding using appropriate statistical methods (Gaussian finite mixture modeling with BIC criterion). The bimodal distribution is well-supported by the data and consistent with prior work (C17, C20). This represents a key discovery of the study.

result: Non-rhythmic and theta-rhythmic HD cells show distinct theta phase relationships but similar local field potential theta power, HD selectivity, and mean firing rates. Non-rhythmic cells show weak but significant theta phase modulation (94.1% of cells).
evaluation: Claims C23-C26 characterize the functional differences between the two HD cell populations. The statistical comparisons are appropriate and demonstrate that differences in theta rhythmicity are not due to recording location or differences in directional tuning strength.

result: Theta-cycle skipping was observed in 10% of theta-rhythmic HD cells, slightly lower than in rats. Analysis of simultaneously recorded cell pairs revealed only one mixed non-rhythmic/theta-rhythmic pair among 17 pairs, suggesting partial anatomical segregation.
evaluation: Claims C27-C29 provide evidence for anatomical segregation of the two cell types. However, the sample size for simultaneous recordings (N=17 pairs) is relatively small, and the inference of anatomical segregation (C29) could benefit from additional evidence.

result: Histological analysis of a subset of animals revealed that non-rhythmic HD cells were recorded from both the MEC (4 of 7 sites) and the postrhinal cortex (3 of 7 sites).
evaluation: Claims C32-C33 are based on a very small sample (7 recording sites) with a biased sampling strategy (stopping experiments early when non-rhythmic cells were found). The finding of non-rhythmic HD cells in postrhinal cortex is interesting but requires further validation with unbiased sampling.

result: Visual landmark manipulations caused significant changes in preferred HD (63.4% of cells) and HD scores (47.3% of cells). Non-rhythmic HD cells showed significantly larger changes in preferred HD than theta-rhythmic cells (p=0.00012).
evaluation: Claims C36-C38 demonstrate a major finding using appropriate statistical methods (shuffling procedure). The differential response between non-rhythmic and theta-rhythmic cells is well-supported and represents a key result of the study.

result: Unlike HD cells in the presubiculum and anterodorsal thalamic nucleus that maintain firing rates across environments, 40.9% of MEC/PaS HD cells significantly altered their mean firing rate in response to visual landmark changes.
evaluation: Claims C40-C41 establish an important difference between MEC/PaS HD cells and classic HD cells in other brain regions. The comparison to prior work (C40) provides appropriate context for interpreting the novel finding (C41).

result: Visual landmark-driven changes in HD cells were not due to altered spatial firing patterns, as 86.1% of non-spatial HD cells showed significant changes. Similarly, 83.6% of MEC-only HD cells displayed significant changes.
evaluation: Claims C44 and C46 address important alternative explanations for the observed effects. The control analyses strengthen the conclusion that visual landmarks directly affect HD cell tuning independent of spatial selectivity or recording location.

result: The tuning curve changes between vp1 and vp2 trials were not explained by changes in tuning curve width or systematic biases in preferred directions toward either visual pattern.
evaluation: Claims C48-C49 rule out alternative explanations for the observed effects, specifically addressing whether visual landmark properties (width, salience) could account for the changes. These control analyses strengthen the main conclusions.

result: Bidirectional HD cells (15.1% of HD cells) showed significant changes in bidirectionality scores between trial types (p=0.009), with non-rhythmic cells showing larger changes than theta-rhythmic cells (p=0.004).
evaluation: Claims C50-C53 characterize a subpopulation of bidirectional HD cells and their response to visual landmarks. The statistical tests are appropriate, though the functional significance of bidirectionality and its relationship to visual landmark control could be explored further.

result: Contrary to attractor network model predictions of coherent HD cell responses, non-rhythmic HD cell pairs showed significant reorganization of firing associations (preferred HD: p=0.01, HD score: p=0.00781, IFR association: p=0.00391), while theta-rhythmic pairs maintained stable associations (all p>0.14).
evaluation: Claims C54-C55, C59-C60 present a major finding that challenges existing theoretical frameworks. The simultaneous recording of cell pairs provides strong evidence for non-coherent reorganization in non-rhythmic cells. This is a key result demonstrating that not all HD cells are constrained by attractor dynamics.

result: HD cell pairs with high theta synchrony (HTS) showed no significant reorganization (all p>0.14), while low theta synchrony (LTS) pairs showed significant reorganization (all p<0.001) in response to visual landmark changes.
evaluation: Claims C61-C62 provide an alternative characterization of HD cell reorganization based on theta synchrony rather than theta rhythmicity. This analysis strengthens the conclusion that synchronized cells maintain coherent responses while non-synchronized cells reorganize.

result: Grid cells (N=219) showed highly preserved firing associations between vp1 and vp2 trials (IFR correlation r=0.96, map similarity r=0.95), with no significant reorganization (p>0.05), contrasting with the significant reorganization observed in HD cells.
evaluation: Claims C63-C69 demonstrate that grid cells maintain stable firing associations despite visual landmark changes, unlike HD cells. This important control shows that the reorganization is specific to HD cells and not a general property of MEC/PaS neurons.

result: The study demonstrates that visual information impacts MEC/PaS HD cells beyond simple anchoring, with a significant proportion expressing a conjunctive code for HD, visual landmarks, and position. Non-rhythmic HD cells are not strictly controlled by attractor-like dynamics and show malleable, landmark-controlled firing associations.
evaluation: Claims C78-C81 present the main conclusions of the study, well-supported by the experimental findings. The evidence for conjunctive coding and the departure from attractor dynamics in non-rhythmic cells represents a significant advance in understanding HD cell function.

result: Comparison with bidirectional HD cells in retrosplenial cortex reveals that while retrosplenial bidirectional cells rotate coherently with each other, MEC/PaS non-rhythmic HD cells show non-coherent reorganization, suggesting greater heterogeneity in cortical HD signals compared to subcortical areas.
evaluation: Claims C82-C85 appropriately contextualize the findings within the broader literature on HD cells. The comparison highlights important differences between brain regions and supports the conclusion of greater heterogeneity in cortical HD representations.

result: Theta-rhythmic HD cells maintain coherent responses to visual landmarks and could provide stable directional input to grid cells, consistent with computational models requiring coherent HD signals for grid cell function.
evaluation: Claims C86-C88, C92 propose a functional role for theta-rhythmic HD cells based on the experimental findings and computational models. The proposal is well-reasoned and supported by the data, though direct evidence for the interaction with grid cells would strengthen this conclusion.

result: Non-rhythmic HD cells may act as an interface between visual landmarks and the coherent HD signal, potentially contributing to setting preferred directions of theta-rhythmic HD cells in new environments and influencing grid cell orientation within modules.
evaluation: Claims C93-C95 present speculative functional interpretations that, while plausible and consistent with the data, lack direct experimental support. These hypotheses would require additional experiments to test the proposed interactions between non-rhythmic and theta-rhythmic cells.

result: Theta-rhythmic and non-rhythmic HD cells likely form anatomically distinct populations with different biophysical properties (spike waveform differences: trough-to-peak duration p<10^-8, asymmetry p=0.002), potentially located in different MEC subregions or layers.
evaluation: Claims C96-C99 provide evidence for anatomical and biophysical distinctions between the two cell types. The spike waveform analysis is convincing, though the anatomical localization (C98-C99) is more speculative and based on limited histological data.

result: MEC/PaS HD cells comprise two functionally distinct types: theta-rhythmic cells that respond coherently to visual landmarks (resembling classic HD cells) and non-rhythmic cells that show larger, non-coherent responses, revealing landmark-driven reorganization within the HD cell population.
evaluation: Claims C100-C103 summarize the main findings of the study. The evidence strongly supports the existence of two functionally distinct HD cell populations with different responses to visual landmarks, representing a major advance in understanding HD cell diversity.

result: Similar to context-dependent reorganization in non-periodic place cells of the MEC, an equivalent reorganization occurs within the MEC/PaS HD code, suggesting a general principle of context-dependent coding in this brain region.
evaluation: Claims C104-C105 place the findings in the broader context of MEC function. The parallel between HD cell reorganization and place cell reorganization suggests common mechanisms for context-dependent coding in the MEC.
